newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian official steps down over swastika.
newsitem.headline: Canadian official steps down over swastika.

text.p: Quebec Lt. Gov. Jean-Louis Roux resigned on Tuesday after disclosing that he wore a swastika, the Nazi symbol, as a student 54 years ago.

Roux, the official representative in Quebec of Britain's Queen Elizabeth, who is Canada's head of state, announced in a one-sentence statement that he had submitted his resignation to Prime Minister Jean Chretien.
"Jean-Louis Roux submitted this morning, to the prime minister of Canada, the Right Honourable Jean Chretien, his resignation as lieutenant-governor of Quebec," it said.

His post is largely ceremonial but he was appointed by Chretien in September and the prime minister's government was hammered about the issue in Parliament on Monday. Chretien spokeswoman Leslie Swartman said the prime minister accepted the resignation. She said he had not pressured Roux to go.

Roux, 74, said he had drawn a swastika on his laboratory coat as a pre-medical student at L'Universite de Montreal in 1942. He also marched in a Second World War anti-draft protest that ended with demonstrators breaking the windows of Montreal shops bearing Jewish-sounding names, but he said he did not take part in the vandalism.

The disclosures were in a magazine article last weekend and prompted howls of outrage in Parliament from the official opposition, the separatist Bloc Quebecois. But Chretien's Liberal ministers defended Roux, saying his actions were the indiscretions of a youth half a century ago.
They added that many Quebeckers had opposed the draft during the war and that Roux had since fought fascism.

Complicating the issue was the fact that Roux had outspokenly opposed Quebec separation from Canada during a referendum on the issue last year, endearing him to Ottawa but alienating him from French-speaking separatists.

The head of the Quebec Liberal Party, Daniel Johnson, said stepping down was Roux's only option. "With all the criticism and requests for explanations of all kinds, the only decision possible by Mr. Roux was this one, and it's the best decision he could make," Johnson said in Quebec City.
